section.title: The harmonic series and first warnings
section.p: The last section gave two friendly kinds of series. A geometric series has partial sums with a formula. A telescoping series has partial sums with cancellation.
Most series are less generous. We often cannot compute
exactly. We need tests that tell whether the partial sums settle down.
The first test is not a convergence test. It is a warning test.
section.md: \text{If an infinite sum converges, the terms being added must become small.}
section.p: That sounds obvious. The danger is the converse. Terms can become small and still add up to infinity.

subsection.title: Terms can go to zero while the series diverges
subsection.p: Look at the series

So each individual term becomes tiny. But the accumulated sum is another question. The first few partial sums are
The partial sums keep increasing. That alone does not prove divergence. They might increase toward a horizontal ceiling, as the geometric partial sums did.
The surprise is that there is no ceiling.
The series
is called the harmonic series. It diverges, even though its terms approach zero.
This is the first essential warning in infinite series:
A term is one small contribution. A series is the accumulated effect of infinitely many contributions. Small pieces can still have an infinite total.

exercise.title: Why can terms go to zero while the series diverges?

statement.p: The harmonic series has terms 1/k\to 0, yet it diverges. In your own words, why is a term only one small contribution, and why can infinitely many shrinking contributions still have an infinite total?

hint.p: Convergence is about accumulated running totals, not about one term becoming tiny. Small pieces can still pile up without a ceiling.

subsection.p: The second form is often called the term test for divergence.
The name matters. It is a divergence test, not a convergence test.
subsection.md: \text{If the terms do not go to zero, the series diverges.}
subsection.p: But if the terms do go to zero, we still do not know.

exercise.title: Why is the term test only a divergence test?

statement.p: If a series converges, then a_k\to 0. Equivalently, if the terms do not approach zero, the series diverges. In your own words, why does that implication run in only one direction, and what has been learned if the terms do go to zero?

hint.p: A necessary condition can rule a series out, but it cannot rule a series in. Passing the first obstacle is not the same as arriving.

example.title: terms go to zero, but the test says nothing

statement.p: The term test gives no conclusion. It does not say the harmonic series converges. It only says that the first obstacle to convergence has been passed.

subsection.title: The harmonic series
subsection.p: The harmonic series is
It is the simplest series whose terms go to zero but whose sum still diverges.
The partial sums grow slowly:
Slow growth can look like convergence if we only compute a few terms. This is a common trap in numerical work. A long plateau is not the same as a limit.
The right proof groups the terms.

subsection.p: This proof is more than a trick. It shows a new habit. When we cannot compute partial sums exactly, we compare them with something simpler.
That is the main idea behind the next tests.

exercise.title: Why does grouping doubled blocks prove harmonic divergence?

statement.p: Grouping the harmonic series into blocks whose lengths double shows that each new block contributes at least 1/2. In your own words, why does that force the partial sums to be unbounded, and what new habit does the argument teach for later tests?

hint.p: Infinitely many blocks of size at least 1/2 cannot have a finite total. When exact partial sums are unavailable, comparison with something simpler becomes the method.
